title: From telephone directories to evidence of service and use
question: What can the New Haven exchange's subscriber list establish about early service, and what independent records establish use or connect the exchange to a particular technical predecessor?
summary: The February 1878 broadside has 50 printed listings, including 11 under Residences, and gives the operator's stated hours. A local newspaper independently reports a March 1880 telephone notification to the Police Office, which had appeared on the 1878 sheet. Coy's 1880 patent describes central switching as a technical operation. The exact opening tally, the route of the 1880 call, and the identity of the January 1878 switch design remain unresolved.
inputs: Operator and all name variants, locality, central-office addresses and claimed milestone dates
Claimed event type and count unit, including date range, geography and denominator if supplied
Candidate earlier technology and later operator or installation, with names of parties involved
Directory, operator, regulator and subscriber archives, plus local newspaper issues

steps.title: Identify the item and its editions
steps.action: Search national telephone-directory collections and the operator's corporate finding aid for the exact firm name plus subscriber list, telephone directory or prospectus. Try company-name variants and search by city and year. Compare title, issue date, publisher, street address and pagination; inspect the facsimile itself. Use catalogue entries to track custody and compare reproductions of the same document.
steps.result: The complete facsimile reads List of Subscribers, New Haven District Telephone Company, 219 Chapel Street, February 21, 1878. Connecticut Humanities credits the UConn Southern New England Telephone Company Records. The Library of Congress gallery indexes a second reproduction as reel 0 905006, frame 12, after an electrostatic reproduction target. The direct UConn object and Library of Congress frame endpoints could not be retrieved. The Seton Guide catalogues the February sheet at HE8841.N322.1878 and under MSS B56. The November 1878 bound directory has a different named publisher and its auction record describes instructions and a later subscriber list. It is a distinct edition.

steps.title: Count listings and read qualifications
steps.action: Count printed rows from the full image by heading and record how addresses, branches, ditto marks, repeated names and carry-over rows are handled. Record hours and other future-tense promises separately from the named entries. Compare names and premises in city directories or subscriber contracts before deduplicating. Obtain a separate dated account register, line book, connection log or defined survey population before claiming the corresponding totals or rate.
steps.result: Visual count of the sheet yielded 11 residence, 3 physician, 2 dentist, 8 miscellaneous, 20 store and factory, 4 market, and 2 stable rows. M. F. Tyler appears under Residences and with Law Chambers under Miscellaneous. New Haven Flour Co. has four location rows, three with ditto marks. Fifty rows count names or listed places; eleven count entries under Residences. Distinct persons, households, premises, paying accounts, active devices or stations, connected lines and completed calls require other sources. The footer gives 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. and announces all-night opening after March 1.

steps.title: Seek a subscriber or independent operating witness
steps.action: Select a distinctive listed institution and search its original minutes, reports, accounts or correspondence and the local press around the claimed installation and subsequent use. Search newspaper OCR by local title, date, central office or telephone exchange and the institution's name or role. Check original page mastheads and whether each result is a paid notice, independent news item or firsthand user report. Record both endpoints and operator, and look for an explicit switching step or circuit identifier.
steps.result: The February sheet includes Police Office under Miscellaneous. In the Chronicling America New Haven newspaper material, searching for telephone and police located a March 23, 1880 news item reporting that word was sent to the police office by telephone during the prior afternoon's recovery of Owen McGrail's body. The story reports the coroner's response and leaves the caller's premises, provider and route unspecified. Separate period newspaper testimony in the September 2, 1886 Evening Mercury reprints a New Haven Register report describing a reporter who spoke from the Southern New England Telephone Company executive office to New York. The demonstrated toll circuit and announced future availability to merchants are separate claims; neither dates the January 1878 local service.

steps.title: Reconcile launch, routine commercial service and adoption
steps.action: Write one claim per date and unit. Mark launch announcements, formal opening, practical connection, payment and ordinary use separately. Trace commemorative figures to original sources and identify repeated reporting or incompatible denominators. Require operating or billing records, contractual performance, or independent direct reporting before converting a claim about listings or availability into actual uptake.
steps.result: De Land retrospectively reports roughly 30 subscribers beginning to receive service January 21 and a formal opening January 28. The National Park Service gives January 28 and 21 initial subscribers. The Census Bureau's later account gives January 25 for opening for business. The Bell Laboratories Record later pairs 21 customers with eight lines, while De Land describes subscribers sharing lines. These accounts leave the first-day tally and comparability unsettled. The February sheet can be counted directly, but does not establish whether all entries were installed, billed or in use, or whether the number of paying accounts doubled. An earlier prospectus makes the failure mode concrete. Kingsbury reproduces Ponton's October 1877 Titusville plan for a central switch room and records Ponton's January 1878 report that he had failed to generate sufficient interest to establish it.

steps.title: Test a named technical dependency from both ends
steps.action: Identify precisely what moved from the source achievement to the recipient, identifying supplier, instrument or design, exact dates and means of transfer. On the supplying side inspect patents, order books or correspondence. On the receiving side inspect a signed agreement, delivery or installation record and a source showing how the specified item or method was used. Test proposed routes against private lines, same-line signaling, message relay and independent design.
steps.result: Bell's 7 March 1876 U.S. patent 174,465, claim 5, describes electric transmission of voice sounds. At the recipient end, the Seton Guide identifies an early local prospectus with Bell authorization in the title, but only the catalogue entry was available. De Land reports use of Bell telephones and the local licence. The evidence makes Bell instrument use credible and leaves the exact instrument or shipment and licence terms unverified from originals. Coy's separate U.S. patent 224,653 describes an attendant joining two circuits so their parties can speak, and postdates the 1878 opening. It provides original technical evidence for Coy's later design, with no match established to January hardware. The 1877 demonstration or the resemblance of earlier telegraph and district call-box systems does not document the transfer of a specific board or switching method to Coy.

steps.title: Close or record the next archival check
steps.action: Write the strongest direct claim, actual use of the specific system if evidenced, and the missing link or denominator. Use the most precise titles and dates for the next search. Separate available scans, catalogue-only material, subscription collections and physical holdings.
steps.result: The New Haven Free Public Library lists Daily Palladium microfilm spanning 1878, and the Yale guide lists online New Haven Register coverage from 1878 through 1900 via a subscription collection. Their original 1878 candidate pages were not inspected. De Land's p. 51 discussion of the November 4 election preparations and subsequent ward-return coverage gives a narrow newspaper search window around November 4–7. Seek the newsroom report and a municipal or operator record explicitly naming the central-office routing and the ward origin. The UConn corporate records and New Haven Museum prospectus entry give routes for licensing or installation records; a city police report or bill could confirm the provider for local use. A later Yale student-magazine article identifies a connection advertisement in the first weeks of the Yale News. The Yale Daily News Historical Archive endpoint returned 403, leaving the ad's precise issue and its relationship to the listed Yale News subscriber unresolved.

reject_if: Reject a service, adoption or transfer inference if all witnesses derive from one operator's publicity, the unit is merely a printed listing, the call route cannot be distinguished from a private circuit, or the earlier design lacks a documented recipient-side connection. A second scan of the same publication counts as the same testimony.
stop_when: Release the date, claim type, geography and count unit that actually survive source comparison. Leave launch-day totals, rates and network attribution open where the relevant ledger, denominator or named routing witness remains missing. Log the issue window, archive and item needed to reopen each decision.
next_anchor: Radiolinja GSM digital mobile service in Finland. Trace the July 1991 ceremonial call separately from terminal approvals and ordinary subscribers, using Finnish regulator licensing or approval records and dated subscriber or billing evidence independent of launch publicity.
decision: Add the February 1878 directory as a dated description with two printed-listing measures and cite the March 1880 report as limited corroboration of local telephone use. Keep the January availability bound, the launch headcount uncertainty and the open question of how the reported police call was routed. Bell telephone use is credible at the instrument-family level. A matched equipment or licensing record is needed to document what Bell supplied to Coy, and the later Coy patent leaves the origin of the January switching design open.
next: Inspect 1878 local news issues and the early company and municipal records for named operator connections, actual intervals of service and identifiable equipment. Reuse the same claim and count-unit checks for Radiolinja.
